Agent Matrix2026Personal project · Multi-agent workflow

I designed how AI asks me. Then I used it to rework this portfolio.

I reworked this portfolio with a group of AI agents. Anything I need to look at or decide reaches me as a card, and only I can give the decision. Over ten days I received 181 of them. This case is about how I designed that card, and how using it every day changed the card itself.

Problem
The agents change things faster than I can review them. Knowing something was waiting on me was not enough: I often could not tell what I was meant to review, and text alone did not let me judge.
Key decisions
I set a fixed format for asking, the review card. Every card answers five questions. I look at the images, annotate and decide on a web page, and my decision and my note go back to the agent that raised the card.
Outcome
Over ten days, 181 portfolio cards went through it. The PlayBook demos, the home-page covers, the split SMT page and the 3D fridge prototype each came from one line I wrote on a card. The friction I hit while using it went back into the tool itself.
Context
Personal project · a multi-agent workflow first built for a game I am making, now used to rework this portfolio
My role
Requirements, trade-off decisions and acceptance; documentation and development in collaboration with Claude
Timeline
Oct 2026 – ongoing
Deliverables
Review centre (live), Feishu board, session renewal, decision dispatch, daily retrospective

01 · Background

It was first built for a game.

This setup was first built for a game. I am making a 2D narrative management game adapted from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland. I am the producer, and 14 Claude agents each own one area. Each agent works in its own session and edits only its own folder. Only I can mark something as approved.

Once the work was split across agents, output jumped. I set up a “waiting on you” table, and by the next morning it had 33 items opened and 22 still open. Questions put to me directly in a session were mostly answered within 20 minutes. The unprompted ones simply stayed open.

After that, each new problem got one new mechanism, nine in all. Four matter most here. A board keeps the plan I set and what each agent is doing right now as two separate layers. The review card fixes how agents ask me. Work runs one batch per session, each ending with one page of state for a clean new session to pick up. And a scheduled dispatch delivers the decisions I have made to the agent that raised the card.

Tobie’s note

The hard part is not getting agents to work. It is getting their questions to reach me in a form I can act on.

02 · Moving to the portfolio

Ten days, 181 cards.

Once the work on this portfolio ran through the same setup, 57 cards arrived on the first day, and 181 over ten days: 93 asking me to choose, 64 to accept a result, 13 to do something myself, and 11 to answer a question.

Every card has to answer five questions: what I am being asked to do, why we are at this point, where to look, what the options are, and what happens once I decide. A card missing any of them is rejected on submission. An agent cannot approve its own work; a decision can only come from me, on the page.

On the page I look at the images, pin notes onto them, write a line and give my decision. The decision and the line are delivered back to the agent that raised the card, which makes the change and submits the next version. Over these ten days, the median time from a card arriving to my first response was 38 minutes.

Tobie’s note

A good question turns “I need to think about this” into “I can decide at a glance.”

03 · What changed

One line from me, one change on the page.

Of the 181, I sent 23 back at least once, and 35 went to a second version or beyond. The four changes below each started from one line I wrote on a card.

PlayBook
“Then we might as well just show the video like before.”
The three demos could only be stepped through in a fixed order. Now a reader can operate them freely, in any order.
Home covers
“Don’t use one style for all of them.”
All four covers used the same layout. PlayBook kept it. Industrial Securities SMT, The Commons Fridge and Qingju each got their own, tied to the project.
SMT
“These are two different trading systems, one on a phone and one on a PC.”
Industrial Securities and Daton Securities were described on one page. The case now opens with two tabs, one for each.
The Commons Fridge
“The UI on this page is too poor. I’ll present it another way; the project is on hold for now.”
That version stopped there. The fridge itself was then rebuilt as a 3D interface, now live.

I sent the covers back three times. One of my replies was: “Honestly, I can’t see it, and I don’t understand what it would look like. If nothing else, make one version of the style and show me.” Twenty-one minutes later the agent came back with three finished covers. I pointed out that one of them hid the page, so it made three variants for each of the three cases. I picked a set four minutes after they arrived.

Tobie’s note

I often cannot say what I want, but I know what is wrong once it is in front of me. The card’s job is to get it there early.

04 · Reframing

I said switching mattered most. 203 cards said otherwise.

Once the review centre was live, I was getting 17 to 57 cards a day. The friction showed up one spot at a time: I wrote a line on a card, and an agent fixed it.

Unreadable on a phone
A card asked me to read a checklist but gave only a path on my computer. I couldn’t open it on my phone, and marked it done without reading it.
Files now travel with the card and open in the page, on a phone too.
Asked twice
Agents asked me again in chat about things I had already answered on the site.
Each card now records which session raised it, and a session checks for my answers before it asks me.
No sense of progress
The progress page was just a list. I couldn’t tell how far things had got or what they looked like now.
Each project got a timeline, and every step opens to what it looks like now.

The biggest one was harder to fix. Each time I handled a card, the queue held a median of 10, that card included, and 61 at the peak. I thought switching between cards was the problem, so I had an agent build a three-pane layout with the list beside the card. I rejected it with one line: don’t assume the problem is defined right; trace the second- and third-order effects.

It went back through the 203 real cards so far, 167 of them from this portfolio. I handled a median of 2 per sitting, 55 seconds apart. 59% of the time I opened the newest card first; I never started with the oldest. 12% were sent back, and 33 needed a second version. Switching was not the slow part. There were too many cards, too fragmented, too hard to read. My own rejection notes said “I don’t know what exactly I’m meant to change” and “I can’t really see a difference.”

It came back with four options, each with its knock-on effects. Three panes would make the card a third narrower, and “I can’t see the difference” was already the most common reason for sending one back. I chose a one-line counter plus fixing the source. It then used the data to overrule two of my picks: acceptance cards with comparison images were sent back more often, not less; and I followed the recommended option only 73% of the time, too low to stop asking me.

What shipped were three small things: “N left · next” at the top of each card; earlier cards on the same thread listed under the header; non-urgent cards older than three days sink to the bottom. I pinned two problems on the first version’s screenshots, and the second version passed.

The source is getting fixed too. Before a new card reaches me, Codex reads it as a reviewer and sends it back if it doesn’t hold up; on its first real run it found four errors in a card I had already approved. On my side, I now get eight seconds to take back a decision, with my comments and annotations restored.

Tobie’s note

What I asked for was a solution, not necessarily my problem.

05 · Next

Fewer things that need me at all.

Everything above makes waiting for me smoother. The deeper fix is to have fewer things wait for me. Two rules now work on that.

The first covers the times I am away. After three days, a non-urgent choice proceeds on the option the card recommends, and I can reverse it when I am back. Of six cards that were waiting on me during the game work, it covers three. The two blocking acceptance cards and the one that needs me to act in person still wait.

The second covers which kinds of work I can look at less. It is a set of trust levels, four of them, set per type of task. At the lowest level the AI states its plan at every step and acts only after I agree. It moves up a level after several consecutive results I did not need to change. Only at the top level can that type of task go into scheduled or batch runs. The approach follows a talk by Lauren Tan; the levels themselves were added by Claude.

Each time I correct something, the correction has to become a rule or a check, not one more sentence in a prompt. Closing an acceptance card writes to the trust ledger on its own: passed first time counts as a pass, sent back counts as a correction. Then the first cell in the ledger moved up. For web-page work, Claude delivered three results in a row that I did not change, and went from “ask before every step” to “act, then show the evidence.”

One thing is still undecided: the scheduled tasks depend on my laptop being awake. Two things to watch next: whether the number of cards I have to decide each day falls as levels rise, and what still stops the next time I am away.

Tobie’s note

Trust is not handed over once. It is earned back, one type of task at a time.
